questions.text: I tend to undercharge or waive fees when someone genuinely cannot afford what I offer.
When I feel overwhelmed, it's not just emotional — my body feels like it's short-circuiting.
A stranger's pain matters to me as much as a friend's.
I want to be the one who shapes how a project unfolds.
I swap seasonal items when the weather actually changes rather than on a set date.
I tend to miss the social significance of who reaches out to whom first after a conflict.
A stranger's obvious anguish in front of me rarely makes me want to step in.
When I receive unexpected praise, the flush of pleasure is so strong it makes me lightheaded.
I hold the view that every person's first responsibility is to themselves.
I find it satisfying to have direct reports and be responsible for their output.
I often find myself hoping that people I hear about who are struggling will be okay.
Even a stranger's serious suffering makes me want to see it relieved.
I notice that confrontations, while unpleasant, don't leave a physiological residue in my body.
I feel responsible for keeping a group connected and cohesive.
I tend to allocate the majority of my time to tasks that benefit other people.
I can tell when someone volunteers information to create an impression of transparency while still hiding the important parts.
I show up to learning experiences fresh, without preparation, to keep my perspective unbiased.
I sense when a conversation partner is mirroring my energy not out of genuine rapport but as a social technique.
I rarely sense when a person's choice of words reveals their stance on an issue they have not explicitly addressed.
I notice micro-expressions that flash across someone's face during conversation.
My emotional baseline is so stable that people often describe me as having a calming presence.
I sit with vague goals and let clarity emerge before forcing them into action steps.
I can still feel the emotional residue of an argument hours or even days later.
I am open to revisiting any decision if the group raises new concerns.
I routinely lend my possessions and rarely ask for them back.
I notice that my emotional life, while not dramatic, is dependable and clear.
I routinely choose solitude for deep personal work over collaboration that dilutes my focus.
I feel most confident when I have rehearsed or prepared thoroughly for an event.
I review my goals regularly and adjust my plans to stay on track.
I am careful to manage my energy across the day so I don't burn out before evening.
I often do not notice when someone feels excluded from a group.
When someone shares a struggle with me, I tend to treat it as information rather than as something that calls for a response.
I have been told that I am a great team player.
I routinely take credit for my contributions because acknowledging my own work matters to me.
Another person's pain rarely feels real enough to matter to me.
I am the person who usually decides how resources get distributed in a group project.
